# Sīlānisaṁsajātaka (Ja 190)
**ID:** Ja 190
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Sīlānisaṁsajātaka
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja190
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Sīlānisaṁsajātaka* (Ja 190), translated as *The Benefits of Morality*, is a birth story in the *Jātaka* collection of the Pali canon [SuttaCentral]. In the Jātaka commentary edited by V. Fausböll, it appears as the tenth story of the *Asadisavagga* [Fausböll 1879]. The narrative opens with the stanza beginning *Passa saddhāya sīlassa* and was recounted by the Buddha at Jetavana concerning a devoted lay disciple (*saddha upāsaka*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In the framing "story of the present" (*paccuppannavatthu*), the lay follower crosses the Aciravatī River to reach Jetavana by walking upon the water through the joy born of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhārammaṇaṁ pītiṁ*), but starts to sink when his concentration slackens at the sight of the waves [Fausböll 1879; Winternitz 1933]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the stream-enterer layman attains the fruit of once-returning (*sakadāgāmiphala*), the Nāga king is revealed to be Sāriputta, and the sea deity (*samuddadevatā*) is identified as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1879].
Maurice Winternitz famously observed that this account in Jātaka No. 190 of walking upon the water through faith provides a striking parallel to the New Testament story of St. Peter walking on the sea in Matthew 14:28ff., arguing that the detailed correspondence between the two legends makes independent origin highly improbable [Winternitz 1933]. Julius Evola likewise references the story to illustrate how supernormal occurrences in early Buddhist texts are explained through mental concentration and the logic of the path rather than as irrational miracles [Evola 1995].
According to DharmaNexus, text reuse aligns this Jātaka with the *Devatā Saṁyutta* of the *Saṁyutta Nikāya* (SN 1), with 12 matching passages (notably the verse segment §2.1–2.3 matching SN 1 §31.4.1–31.4.3), along with extensive verbatim sharing with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies parallels in non-Pali canonical collections [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Devatā Saṁyutta (SN 1) (§2.1–2.3 ↔ §31.4.1–31.4.3); Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Dutiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a2) (§0.4–2.4 ↔ §683–687)
